title: SMTP Service Extension for Secure SMTP over Transport Layer Security
summary: Describes the STARTTLS extension to SMTP, which lets a mail client and server upgrade a plain connection to one protected by TLS. This provides privacy and optional authentication against eavesdroppers. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Two mail programs start talking out loud, then agree to switch to a secret code so nobody listening can understand. This is how they ask each other to switch.

questions: how to encrypt smtp with tls
subtitle: How an SMTP client and server upgrade a plain-text mail connection to one protected by TLS.

tldr.problem: SMTP servers and clients normally talk in the clear, often across routers that neither side controls or trusts, so a third party can watch or alter the mail traffic and neither side can prove who it is talking to.
tldr.mechanism: The server advertises a STARTTLS keyword in its EHLO reply. The client sends the new STARTTLS command, the server answers 220, and both sides run a TLS handshake on the same connection and then restart the SMTP session.
tldr.outcome: Each hop can get privacy and optional authentication, but only for that one hop, and an attacker who strips the STARTTLS offer can force the session to stay in the clear unless the endpoints are configured to require TLS. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2487 and is itself updated by RFC 7817.

today: RFC 3207 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2487 and is updated by RFC 7817, so read the two together.

sections.title: Why SMTP Needs TLS
sections.content:
SMTP servers and clients normally communicate in the clear over the Internet. Along the way the traffic may pass through one or more routers that neither side controls or trusts, and such a router could let a third party monitor or alter the conversation.

There is also often a wish for two SMTP agents to authenticate each other. A secure server might accept mail only from agents it knows, or treat known agents differently from unknown ones. TLS (Transport Layer Security, more commonly known as SSL) is the popular mechanism for adding privacy and authentication to TCP connections, and RFC 3207 defines how SMTP uses it. The document obsoletes RFC 2487.
sections.eli5: Mail normally travels like a postcard that anyone along the way could read. TLS is a way to put it in a locked envelope instead.

sections.title: The STARTTLS Extension
sections.content:
The extension is small. The name of the service is STARTTLS, the EHLO keyword is STARTTLS and it has no parameters, a new SMTP verb STARTTLS is defined, and no parameters are added to any other SMTP command.

A server that lists the keyword in its reply to EHLO is telling the client that it is currently able to negotiate TLS. The STARTTLS command itself takes no parameters.
sections.eli5: The server holds up a sign that says "I can do secret code". The client can then ask to switch.

sections.title: The STARTTLS Command
sections.content:
After the client sends STARTTLS, the server replies with one of three codes: 220 (ready to start TLS), 501 (syntax error, no parameters allowed) or 454 (TLS not available due to a temporary reason). After a 220, the client MUST start the TLS negotiation before giving any other SMTP command. If some failure stops it from starting the handshake, it SHOULD abort the connection. With pipelining, STARTTLS must be the last command in a group.

If the client gets a 454, local policy decides what happens next. A client that wanted TLS only for authentication might carry on. A client that wanted encryption must choose between sending anyway without TLS, trying again later, or giving up and telling the sender.

A publicly-referenced SMTP server, meaning one on port 25 of a host listed in the MX record (or A record) for the domain of an address, MUST NOT require STARTTLS in order to deliver mail locally. This protects the interoperability of the Internet's mail system. A server that is not publicly referenced may demand TLS first and SHOULD answer every command other than NOOP, EHLO, STARTTLS or QUIT with 530 Must issue a STARTTLS command first.
sections.eli5: The client says "let's switch" and the server says "go ahead". If the server says "not right now", the client has to decide whether to talk out loud anyway, wait, or give up.

sections.title: After the TLS Handshake
sections.content:
Once the handshake finishes, both parties MUST immediately decide whether to continue, based on the authentication and privacy they actually got. They may carry on even with neither, because most SMTP is done without either, but one side may want a minimum level. A client that is unhappy SHOULD send QUIT straight away. A server that is unhappy SHOULD answer every command except QUIT with 554.

The SMTP protocol is then reset to its initial state. The server MUST discard anything it learned from the client before TLS, such as the argument to EHLO, and the client MUST discard what it learned from the server, such as the list of extensions. The client SHOULD send EHLO again as its first command. The new extension list MAY differ, for example because a server only offers a particular SASL mechanism after seeing a client certificate.

Neither side may start TLS twice: a client MUST NOT try to start a TLS session if one is already active, and a server MUST NOT offer STARTTLS in an EHLO reply after the handshake. The RFC also notes that STARTTLS is valid on the Submission port and can be especially useful there, since that port is by definition not publicly referenced.
sections.eli5: After the switch, both sides forget everything they said in the open and start the conversation over in the secret code, just to be safe.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SMTP is not end to end. Adding TLS between one pair of servers does not protect the whole delivery chain, because a message may pass between more than two servers. Even if a server can authenticate a client, that says nothing about whether the client authenticated the author of the mail.

Both sides must check the result of the TLS negotiation, and ignoring this step completely invalidates using TLS for security. There are also man-in-the-middle attacks: an attacker can delete the 250 STARTTLS line so the client never tries TLS, or alter the client's request and the server's response. To defend against these, clients and servers MUST be able to be configured to require successful TLS with an appropriate cipher suite for selected hosts. Offering TLS when possible SHOULD also be provided, and an implementation MAY remember that TLS was used with a peer and warn if it is not used later.

Everything before the handshake is in the clear and can be modified by an active attacker, which is why both sides MUST discard what they learned before TLS began.

STARTTLS is not suitable for authenticating the author of a message unless every hop is authenticated. The RFC points to SMTP-AUTH and to MIME security multiparts for that, and says SASL EXTERNAL MAY be used together with STARTTLS to provide an authorization identity.
sections.eli5: The locked envelope only protects one leg of the trip, and a sneaky person can try to stop the two sides from ever agreeing to lock it. So careful mail programs can be set to refuse to talk unless the lock is used.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2487
sections.content:
RFC 3207 is a revision of RFC 2487. The appendix lists the changes: more discussion of the man-in-the-middle attacks, additional discussion of when a server should and should not advertise STARTTLS, and changed requirements on clients after a 220 response.

It also clarifies how certificates are verified, adds the section on STARTTLS on the Submission port, fixes the usage example so that the client issues a new EHLO, clarifies the paragraph on acceptable degree of privacy, and updates a reference from RFC 821 to RFC 2821.
sections.eli5: This is a cleaned-up second edition of the older rules, with the security warnings and the example fixed.

items.label: Ready to start TLS
items.desc: Reply to STARTTLS; the client must now start the TLS negotiation.

items.label: Syntax error
items.desc: No parameters are allowed on STARTTLS.

items.label: TLS not available
items.desc: Due to a temporary reason; the client decides what to do by local policy.

items.label: Must issue a STARTTLS command first
items.desc: A non-public server that requires TLS answers most commands with this.

items.label: Command refused
items.desc: A server unhappy with the achieved security replies with this to everything but QUIT.
